How CurveSmash works

Choose a target and propose an algorithm that solves it with less total computation. All targets use their full production parameters.

  1. Describe the attack. Specify the algorithm, justify its success probability and account for all its work.
  2. Submit the evidence. Include the written argument and any declared experiments or certificates.
  3. Review, then promotion. One AI reviewer evaluates the complete claim, including objections and responses. At most one follow-up is allowed. Promotion remains a separate human decision in Yukon.

A concrete, supported claim with no confirmed fatal flaw receives its submitted computation bound as the score. Remaining uncertainty is published. Supported heuristic attacks are eligible; formal proof certification is not required.

Read the participant guide

Review process

One AI reviewer examines the algorithm, success probability, complete cost calculation and supporting evidence. It considers objections and their strongest evidence-based responses, with at most one follow-up.

Concrete, supported claims with no surviving fatal flaw may qualify. Supported heuristic attacks are eligible; a Lean proof is not required. Material uncertainty is recorded with the review.

Acceptance means plausible_not_refuted, not mathematical proof, novelty or a practical break. Human promotion in Yukon remains separate.

Participant guideParticipation terms

    

  

  
Cost rules

    
The score is log₂(total computation in target-group-operation equivalents). Lower is better. One reference operation costs 1; other work costs R/C.

    
Fixed reference prices
TrackReference operationC
secp256k1 discrete logarithmBatched incomplete affine addition1,000
BLS12-381 G1 discrete logarithmBatched incomplete affine G1 addition2,000
BLS12-381 pairing inversionDense Fp12 multiplication20,000
BLS12-381 Miller inversionDense Fp12 multiplication20,000

    
R counts scalar AArch64 instruction-equivalent work, including arithmetic, loads, stores, addressing and control. Account for larger arithmetic through its implementation. An analytical calculation is sufficient; assembly and a full-size run are not required.

    
G1 addition uses batched incomplete affine 6M: 3M for the formula and 3M for batch amortisation, with S=M and A=0. There is no standalone field inversion charged per addition. A=0 applies to this reference formula, not to unrelated work.

    
The prices are rounded from pinned real implementations: Bitcoin Core’s field multiplication measures 179 instructions, so 6M is 1,074; blst’s base-field multiplication measures 383, so 6M is 2,298; dense blst Fp12 multiplication measures 22,996. C is fixed at 1,000, 2,000 and 20,000 respectively. These are normalization constants, not CPU timings.

    
For H reference operations and R other instruction equivalents, total work is W(n)=H(n)+R(n)/C. All three BLS tracks submit time_log2=log₂(W(2²⁰)). Explain W(n), its valid range and any number-theoretic conditions.

    
Include preprocessing, advice construction, all attempts and failures, randomness, sorting, lookup, transfers, verification and output. Sum work across processors and count each operation once. Supplied powers are organizer inputs: generating them is excluded, but every access and processing step by the attack counts. A subset may be used.

    
Success must be at least 39% over the specified random challenges and fresh algorithm coins. Report peak memory separately; it adds no scalar penalty or tie-break. Supported heuristics are eligible. Quantum algorithms are outside this classical benchmark.
